title: Regulator-Grade Black Box for Collections Voice Agents
one_liner: A vendor-neutral audit layer that records, checks and attests every AI collections call so lenders can prove the bot behaved.
customer: Mid-size Indian NBFCs, microfinance institutions, digital lenders and collection BPOs running voice AI (Mahindra Finance alone runs about 10M AI calls across 12 languages). The voice-AI vendors selling to them are a channel partner.
problem: Regulators penalize the lender, not the software vendor, for harassment, off-hours calls (RBI allows recovery contact roughly 8am-7pm), third-party contact and false promises. A hallucinated 'your loan is waived' or a threatening tone is a compliance event. No human team can audit millions of calls in 12 languages. Household debt stress is rising (Indonesia paylater defaults, Brazil 82% household-debt indicator), so collection volume and scrutiny are both increasing.
solution: A third-party layer that ingests call audio or streams, runs in-language policy checks (hours, DND and consent status, forbidden phrases, promise-making, tone) and writes a hash-chained call ledger. Native-speaker reviewers sample 1-3% of flagged calls. Each month it issues a regulator-ready attestation pack with violation rates by vendor and script version. Lenders can gate scripts or vendors on the scores, and insurers of the vendors can use the same pack.
why_now: Indian voice-AI orchestration has exploded (Ringg, Bolna, Gnani, Blue Machines) and lenders now run millions of AI calls. ISO's gen-AI exclusions and Verisk's agentic exclusions are pushing carriers to demand evidence before covering AI conduct. Rising defaults in Indonesia and Brazil mean the same product exports.
revenue_model: Per-call-minute fee (roughly Rs 0.10-0.30) or annual attestation subscription of Rs 15-50 lakh per lender, plus a reseller margin through voice-AI vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The vendor can never be its own auditor, and the buyer's budget comes from penalty avoidance, not from a tech line. That makes this a compliance-assurance purchase like a statutory audit, which is stickier and higher-priced than a monitoring dashboard. Whoever becomes the accepted attestor also becomes the data source insurers price from.
first_30_days: Offer a free retrospective audit of 10,000 already-recorded calls to three NBFCs or collection BPOs. Build it on open ASR plus a rules library in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil, with two native reviewers. Deliver a violations report to the chief compliance officer, then convert to a monthly attestation contract.

title: Shift-Matched Nurse Households Near Hospitals
one_liner: Master-lease three- and four-bedroom units near hospitals and match two single-parent nurses with interlocking shifts and similar-aged kids into one household, so overnight and early-morning care is built into the lease. The hospital pays for placement.
customer: Hospitals and health systems (per-placement or per-retained-nurse fee from recruitment and retention budgets), landlords in lease-up (guaranteed master-lease rent), and nurses (their half of rent).
problem: Single parents spend about 35% of income on childcare and the licensed system barely operates at night or on rotating schedules. Nurses' 12-hour rotating shifts do not fit center hours. Turnover of a bedside RN costs a hospital roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile large units near hospitals sit vacant behind concessions, and middle-income renters' late payments rose from 14.3% to 21.6% in a year.
solution: The platform (backed by the hospital's guarantee) master-leases large units from landlords for 12-24 months, then matches nurses on compatible shift patterns, school zone and child ages, with background checks, a shared household agreement, and an optional paid caregiver pool for overlap gaps. Each household pays about half the rent it would pay alone and has an adult at home when the other is at work. Students, residents and travel nurses can fill spare rooms.
why_now: Concessions of 15-37% and 7% vacancy make landlords eager for a guaranteed 12-24 month lease with a hospital-backed credit. Hospitals face the weakest cost position in years (Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027 hit margins of expansion-state hospitals) and cannot afford travel-nurse premiums. Childcare costs are the top named barrier for early-career nurses.
revenue_model: Hospital fee per placed household (about $300-500 a month, justified by retention), plus a 10-15% spread on master-lease rent and caregiver-payroll fees.
non_obvious_insight: Matching on shift patterns is an algorithmic problem no housing platform solves: two nurses on opposite shifts convert the biggest cost in a household (childcare) into an internal schedule, and a hospital's guarantee turns a risky sublease into a credit-enhanced master lease that landlords will happily take at a discount.
first_30_days: Sign a pilot with one hospital's recruitment team and two landlords near campus. Master-lease two 3BR units and recruit four nurse parents from unit-level staffing forums. Write a household agreement and a safety-screening protocol with a family lawyer. Measure retention and shift coverage at 6 months.

title: Legal Price Bargaining Co-ops for Salmon Fleets
one_liner: Back-office software and staff that let independent salmon boats negotiate price as one bloc under the 1934 Fishermen's Collective Marketing Act, as the Bering Sea crab fleet already does.
customer: Member-owned fishermen's associations, starting with one district of 150-400 permit holders that sells to only 1-3 buyers (a Kodiak, Chignik, Cook Inlet, Prince William Sound or Southeast group, not Bristol Bay first). The association pays us. Its dues are collected as a small settlement deduction, about 0.25-0.5% of landed value.
problem: A salmon fisherman is a price-taker. The processor posts a base price and a bonus schedule in June, the boat delivers before it knows the final price, and the retros show up months later. Bristol Bay's average ex-vessel price went from $1.03 in 2025 to $1.72 in 2026, and 2026's $260M fishery came off only 30.1M fish. Nobody on the fishing side of that swing had a seat at the table. Meanwhile most skippers believe acting together is illegal price fixing, so the bar talk about a tie-up dies every spring.
solution: A compliance-first toolkit for member-owned associations. It includes counsel-reviewed charter and bylaw templates under 15 U.S.C. 521-22 and CFEC permit verification at sign-up. Members can vote by SMS. A firewalled clean team collects member-submitted price, volume and quality data. From that it builds a formula price tied to public benchmarks (wholesale frozen sockeye quotes, roe prices, yen and euro, canned prices) plus a quality bonus schedule. We supply the negotiators, contract templates (multi-year formula price, settlement deadlines, audit rights) and dues collection through settlement deductions. The association is the bargaining party and we are the vendor, so we never bargain or set prices ourselves.
why_now: The 2025 crash and 2026 rebound showed the fleet how much money moves on one posted number. Processors now compete with loyalty and quality bonuses (for example $0.15 for RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling). Bonuses are a formula, and formulas can be negotiated. Cheap e-sign, SMS voting and LLM contract review make an association nearly free to run. The crab fleet's Alaska Marketing Association proves the model works in Alaska.
revenue_model: $2-5K/month retainer per association, or 10-15% of dues. On a $260M fishery, 0.25% dues is about $650K/year, so a full-district association is a $65-100K/year account. Later add multi-association benchmarking subscriptions and negotiation-support fees tied to price gains.
non_obvious_insight: The FCMA has let fishermen, not processors, bargain collectively since 1934. The fear that bargaining equals price fixing comes from the DOJ case where processors were the defendants (Pan Alaska Fisheries). Associations fail on operations, not law: no clean data, no dues collection, no fast votes, no credible fallback. Outsiders assume the fleet lacks leverage, but what it lacks is a secretary's office with software.
first_30_days: Pay an antitrust and fisheries lawyer $10-15K for a 10-page FCMA playbook. Pick one small port with a near-monopsony buyer and hold 10 harbor and Facebook-group sessions. Get 30-50 permit holders to sign a non-binding letter of intent. Run a members-only survey of what each boat was actually paid, timed for settlement season (Oct-Dec). Publish a 'your fleet vs. the benchmark' report. Aim for one association signed at a $2K/month retainer by February, before prices post in late spring.

title: CMMC Enclave for CNC Shops
one_liner: A prebuilt, shop-floor-aware CUI enclave and evidence pack that gets 20-person machine shops through CMMC Level 2 without rebuilding their IT.
customer: Job shops and small manufacturers making parts for defense primes (castings, forgings, machined parts), roughly 30,000-plus firms in the defense supply base.
problem: CMMC Level 2 assessments for contract awards ramp up from Nov 2026 (verify dates). Shops keep CUI drawings on machine-side PCs and USB sticks, and generic CMMC consultants scope the entire company. Sub-tier suppliers lack IT staff and capital, exactly the bottleneck AIA-Bain describes.
solution: A managed enclave that isolates only the CAD/CAM and CNC controllers handling CUI, ships as a pre-configured appliance plus cloud tenant, and comes with policies, evidence collection and assessor liaison. Fixed monthly price, no consultants hourly.
why_now: Phase-in of the CMMC rule puts assessment on contracts through 2026-27, and primes are pushing flow-down requirements. Sub-tier financing is scarce, so shops need a low-capex option.
revenue_model: $800-2,500 per month per shop plus $5-15K onboarding. Channel through primes who will subsidize their suppliers' compliance.
non_obvious_insight: Scope reduction is the whole business. The winning product understands machine tool OT and draws a tight boundary around it, while horizontal CMMC vendors sell a heavy enterprise program.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 shops through a regional manufacturing extension partnership. Assemble the appliance from commodity parts. Sign one prime's supplier program as channel.

title: Dock Tax: Pricing Every Shipper Facility's Hidden Premium
one_liner: Use pooled broker quote and cover data to compute the exact per-load premium carriers add to any lane touching each bad dock, then sell shippers a ranked 'fix these five docks' report with dollar savings attached.
customer: VPs of supply chain and transportation procurement at mid-market shippers with $5M-$80M in truckload spend across 8-100 facilities (food and beverage, building products, paper and packaging, PE-backed manufacturers). Secondary: PE operating partners. A second product goes to brokers as a pre-quote facility difficulty score.
problem: Shippers think their rates reflect lane and market. Brokers know the rate also carries a facility premium for long dwell, no appointments, lumper games, no restrooms or parking, and dock staff who vanish at lunch. Our quotes to those docks quietly run $50-$300 a load higher, or the load is skipped by carriers and covered at the last minute at a spot premium. The shipper never sees it because it is buried in the broker's margin, and the broker profits from it, so the broker will never tell them.
solution: Pool anonymized quote-request, time-to-cover, rate-versus-benchmark and carrier-decline-reason data from 10-30 participating small brokers, who get a free facility difficulty score for pre-quoting in return. Run a regression of rate against market benchmark with facility fixed effects. Add dwell data from ELD partners or driver surveys. Deliver a Dock Tax Report: per-facility annualized premium in dollars, ranked, with a fix playbook (appointment windows, extended hours, drop-trailer conversion, driver amenities, lumper policy) and a re-bid plan on the affected lanes.
why_now: Driver supply has tightened through 2025-26 enforcement (English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement, non-domiciled CDL restrictions, authority revocations), which makes carriers pickier about which docks they will visit. AI arrival prediction and automated detention data from TMS integrations are making dwell data cheap. Vendor sources report that moving from first-come-first-served to scheduled appointments cuts dwell 30-50% within about 90 days, so the fix is proven and the ROI is easy to state.
revenue_model: $15K-$40K per shipper report or quarterly engagement, or 15-20% of first-year verified savings. Broker-side subscription of $200-$500/month for pre-quote facility scores builds the data flywheel.
non_obvious_insight: The dock tax is the only freight cost that is invisible to the payer and visible to everyone else. Every broker keeps a mental list of facilities where they never quote under a floor, and colleagues have nicknames for them, but nobody has priced that list for the shipper. Shippers will trust a neutral third party far more than their own broker, because the broker earns from the premium.
first_30_days: Get 8 brokers to share 90 days of anonymized quote and cover data for 20 named facilities in a shared sheet. Build the first regression by hand in a notebook. Cold-message 30 transportation directors on LinkedIn with a free 'your three worst docks' teaser built from the pooled data and public driver reviews, and sell 3 pilots at $7.5K. Give contributing brokers a per-facility difficulty lookup so they keep feeding the pool.

title: Satellite-Armed Sprinklers With Insurer-Grade Uptime Logs
one_liner: A satellite-backed controller that lets a homeowner arm, pre-wet and prove the working state of exterior ember sprinklers after the cell tower and power are gone.
customer: Exurban owners in Colorado foothills and Sierra or Northern California with private water tanks, pumps and exterior sprinkler systems. Installers are the channel, and regional insurers or MGAs that offer mitigation credits are the second payer.
problem: Wildfire defence fails at the exact moment cell towers burn and power drops, and app-based remote activation depends on cellular. Mitigation credits are unclaimable in practice because owners cannot document that a system was armed and working ('1,000 bucks towards a $75,000 metal roof'), and the retrofit baseline is already $8K-$25K.
solution: A $400-$600 controller sits between the pump, valve and battery. It uses LTE-M as primary and NB-NTN satellite as fallback (Skylo or Iridium NTN Direct), sending a daily signed heartbeat of tank level, pump power, valve state and battery in about 50 bytes. The owner can arm or pre-wet by satellite message from an evacuation route, and fire-hotspot feeds (VIIRS, plus FireSat data as it opens up) trigger arm prompts. The signed uptime log exports as documented mitigation for insurer credits and appeals.
why_now: NB-NTN-capable cellular IoT chips (for example Nordic's nRF9151) are shipping, and Iridium NTN Direct launches in 2026, so a satellite fallback is now a chip option rather than a custom radio. Colorado HB25-1182 has required insurers to credit documented mitigation and offer appeals since July 1, 2026. FireSat's first three operational satellites reached orbit in July 2026. Roughly 1-2 kbps satellite links are enough for a 50-byte payload.
revenue_model: $499 hardware plus $19/month service. A 15% referral fee to installers on attach sales. A per-home-per-year data fee of about $25-$50 from insurers or MGAs that accept the log as verified mitigation.
non_obvious_insight: The insurance value is not the sprinkler. It is credible evidence that the sprinkler was armed and worked, and only a device whose telemetry travels on an independent path is believable when everything terrestrial is down. Bandwidth is almost irrelevant, so this is a sub-$5/month satellite bill rather than a broadband product.
first_30_days: Buy 20 NB-NTN dev kits with a Skylo plan and wire them to pump controllers. Sign one Front Range or Sierra sprinkler installer with about 50 existing customers, and put the log format in front of one regional insurer's mitigation-credit desk to test whether it counts. Sell 10 pilot units at $299, and fall back to selling on function alone if no insurer credits it yet.

title: Aftermarket Support for Stranded DJI Fleets
one_liner: Repair, rebuilt batteries, parts and firmware-independence retrofits for the many legally owned DJI drones that can no longer be replaced with new models.
customer: Police and fire drone units, agricultural spray operators, land surveyors, roofing and solar inspectors, and small public-safety departments with grant money.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in December 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in September 2026 (component tariffs follow in 2027), and China's export controls now cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Existing fleets stay legal to fly but face scarce parts and no assured US repair path.
solution: A US repair depot with stocked parts, rebuilt batteries using allied-source cells, gimbal and camera swaps, and open flight-controller retrofits (ArduPilot/PX4) as a migration path. Offer a per-drone maintenance plan with predictive service, and trade-in credits toward US-made airframes, which also become a lead source for those makers.
why_now: The December 2025 FCC action, September 2026 tariffs and export controls all landed within a year. The installed base is large and aging, and no one has a business focused on serving it.
revenue_model: $150-800 per repair, $30-80 per drone per month for maintenance plans, battery and parts sales, and referral fees from US airframe makers on trade-ins.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone debates who replaces DJI, while nobody serves the installed base for the next 5 years. Service earns higher margin than building a competing airframe, starts faster, and gives you the customer list every US-made airframe maker wants.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken Mavic and Matrice units on secondary markets and set up a bench. Pitch fixed-price maintenance plans to 30 sheriff drone units and agricultural spraying co-ops, and sell the first 10 plans.

title: Independent Accuracy Certification for Wearable Health Claims
one_liner: A third-party lab that certifies wearable metrics (HRV, sleep staging, BP trends) now that the FDA has stepped back, funded by makers and trusted by buyers.
customer: Wearable and health-app makers selling into employers, payers, clinics, coaches and gyms (they pay for certification). Secondary: self-insured employers, payers and coaching platforms that subscribe to procurement-grade reports.
problem: Insiders cheered the FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance as freedom. But no clearance means no trusted filter: buyers cannot tell which of dozens of rings, watches and patches are accurate, one analysis argued wearables 'beat the FDA and lost the insurance money', and makers have no credible third-party proof to show payers. Claims exposure to the FTC, state AGs and class actions rises at the same time.
solution: Run a standing panel of about 200 volunteers with lab-grade references (ECG chest strap, a partner polysomnography lab, clinical and ambulatory BP, VO2/lactate testing). Test devices and features under a published protocol, issue tiered 'Verified for [metric]' marks with stated error bands (re-tested at major firmware changes), publish a public leaderboard, and sell buyers a procurement report they can cite in RFPs.
why_now: FDA's Jan 2026 wellness guidance lets physiologic-metric features (HRV, SpO2, BP trends) skip review; Whoop's BP feature drew a July 2025 warning letter and a June 2026 closeout; the HIPRA consumer-health-data bill cleared Senate HELP 22-0 on July 30, 2026, so scrutiny of wearable data is rising while the FDA filter is gone.
revenue_model: Certification fees of $15-60k per device or feature per year with re-test fees; $5-25k/yr buyer subscriptions for procurement reports; per-test fees for startups needing payer credibility.
non_obvious_insight: Deregulation does not remove the need for a trust filter, it privatizes it. The certifier is paid by makers but its only currency is buyer trust, so it must publish unflattering results (Consumer Reports crossed with a safety-lab model). Whoever writes the reference protocol first gets cited in payer and employer RFPs, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Partner with a university exercise-physiology or sleep lab, recruit 40 volunteers, test 6 popular rings/watches on resting HR, HRV and sleep staging against ECG/PSG, publish the methodology and preliminary results, then sell 2-3 employer-facing wearable startups a paid $15k pre-publication verification.

title: Inventory Clearinghouse for Game Stores
one_liner: A store-to-store exchange and standing bid desk that converts hobby shops' slow-moving sealed product into cash or swaps for what customers actually want.
customer: Independent local game stores and card shops (several thousand in the US) that must keep buying broadly to hold their Pokemon and Magic allocation, plus small online breakers who buy sealed at a discount.
problem: The story insiders tell is scarcity: allocation cuts, scalpers, sell-outs. But distributors allocate hot product by account history and volume, so stores end up holding lines they cannot move. Wizards is shipping 7 standard sets in 2026, four of them crossovers (TMNT, Marvel, The Hobbit, Star Trek), and ICv2 reports Pokemon flippers melting down. Cash gets trapped in cold SKUs while the hot ones are short.
solution: A web and SMS app where a store lists overstock (photos, case counts) and sees standing bids from a vetted pool of other stores, breakers and wholesalers. It also finds swaps, such as your Marvel cases for my Pokemon boxes at an index price built from public sold data. We hold payment in escrow, consolidate freight, and guarantee a 72-hour bid on the top ~200 SKUs.
why_now: 2026 has the highest Magic set count ever, and Universes Beyond is now half the calendar. The Pokemon flipper meltdown is compressing secondary margins. Tariffs raised landed costs, so dead stock hurts more. Whatnot's commission change hit existing sellers on 21 Sept 2026, so breakers are hunting cheaper sealed supply.
revenue_model: 3-6% fee on cleared trades, a freight-consolidation margin, and $49/month for bid-desk analytics. Later, short-term working-capital advances against listed inventory.
non_obvious_insight: The same distributor system that starves stores of hot product forces them to carry cold product, and neither distributors nor publishers profit from store-to-store liquidity, so nobody has built it. Stores rarely compete with each other across metros, so they will trade. The clearing spread is the business.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 stores in 2-3 adjacent metros through owner Discords and Facebook groups. Run a manual weekly bid sheet on 30 SKUs using a spreadsheet and Stripe. Spend $30k of your own money on 20 cases of the worst-moving product and resell them to online breakers. First fee revenue by week 3.

title: Placement Exchange for Clients PE Firms Shed
one_liner: A compliant offboarding and warm-handoff service that places small clients dropped by PE-backed accounting firms with vetted independent bookkeepers.
customer: PE-backed and roll-up accounting platforms that raise fee minimums and prune small clients, and independent bookkeepers, enrolled agents and CPAs who want more clients.
problem: PE roll-ups push firms toward larger clients (prior knowledge, not re-verified), so thousands of micro-clients get a 30-day termination letter with scattered records. The exiting firm has E&O and reputation exposure, and the clients don't know where to go. Independent shops want clients but cannot find or vet them. CPA supply is flat at about 678,000.
solution: An offboarding workflow for the shedding firm: client consent, export of prior-year returns and workpapers, engagement-letter templates, and a warm handoff to independents matched on industry, software, language and location. Receiving firms are vetted and rated, and there is a service-level guarantee if the client is unhappy.
why_now: Multi-year PE consolidation of accounting firms continues, AI reduces cost-to-serve for large clients faster than small ones, and the CPA pipeline is flat while demand is projected to rise.
revenue_model: $150-400 per placed client from the receiving firm, $50-100 per client offboarding fee from the shedding firm, and later 8-10% of first-year fees as a recurring referral.
non_obvious_insight: For the roll-up, shedding small clients is an unpriced cost center with legal exposure, so it will pay for graceful exits. The demand side is a waiting list of independents.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 independent bookkeepers and EAs as the buyer panel. Approach operations leaders at five regional roll-ups and offer a free pilot for 50 pruned clients. Build the export checklist and record acceptance and satisfaction rates.

title: Design-for-Duty: Engineer Below the 15% Metal Line
one_liner: A CAD/BOM tool that redesigns imported products to fall under Section 232's metal-weight cliffs or qualify for the 10% US-melt rate.
customer: Product-engineering and sourcing leads at $20M-$500M brands that import metal-heavy goods (furniture, fitness gear, grills, hand tools, lighting, enclosures, HVAC accessories).
problem: Since 2026-04-06 metals duties apply to full customs value: 50% on primary metal, 25% on derivatives, and 10% if made with US-melted steel or US-smelted aluminum/copper. Products under 15% metal weight are excluded (per Foley; verify current text). More derivative articles were proposed on 2026-08-06. Insiders treat this as a sourcing or lobbying problem. Brokers and freight forwarders cannot change a bill of materials, and engineers do not know the cliff exists.
solution: A plugin and standalone tool that ingests CAD mass properties and the BOM (SolidWorks, Fusion, Onshape or CSV). It computes metal weight share per SKU and simulates variants, such as a polymer or wood part in place of a steel bracket, or one US-melted component. It returns duty-weighted landed cost per variant and drafts the engineering change order. It also flags SKUs sitting just above a tier boundary.
why_now: The IEEPA tariffs fell on 2026-02-20 and the regime moved onto Section 232. Metal content is now the biggest variable in landed cost. Full-value duties began in April 2026, and the August 2026 proposal adds derivative products.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-4k a month per product line. Launch-phase audits at $1.5k per SKU. Optional 10-15% share of first-year duty saved on redesigned SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: The tariff is a bill-of-materials problem, not a country problem. A few points of mass shifted can be worth more than moving a factory, and no one in the chain (broker, freight forwarder, sourcing agent) is paid to touch the design.
first_30_days: Pull public bill-of-lading data for HTS chapters exposed to metal derivatives. Cold-email 100 product heads offering a free one-SKU cliff check. Sell 10 fixed-price SKU audits at $1.5k, done in a spreadsheet. Retain a customs attorney to confirm how metal weight is measured. Build the plugin once patterns repeat.

title: Prospecting for Brackish Aquifers Like Gold
one_liner: A water-exploration company that maps, options and permits high-yield brackish and fresh aquifers before developers need them, then sells or leases 'water-ready' sites and supply.
customer: Data-center developers, small towns and rural districts, ranchers and industrial parks needing 1-5 MGD of defensible supply. Buyers pay for studies, and later for site options and supply contracts.
problem: About 1,800 ERCOT projects are held, and water is the new gating item. Siting decisions are still made on power and fiber first, and water studies come late from generalist consultants. Groundwater in Texas is private property under the rule of capture subject to local district rules (my understanding), so early options on proven supply are valuable, yet almost nobody is exploring for water the way miners explore for minerals.
solution: Use public airborne-electromagnetic surveys, well logs and machine learning to map the probability of high-yield brackish aquifers. Option land and water rights, drill test wells, obtain production permits, and pair with a treatment partner. Sell paid site reports first, then options and long-term supply.
why_now: Drone-borne electromagnetic surveys are getting cheap, brackish desalination costs are falling, and regulators are blocking new load without a proven water plan.
revenue_model: $15-75k paid site studies, drilling programs on cost-plus or success fee, and $1-5M site-option or supply sales.
non_obvious_insight: Water rights are the new mineral rights. The geophysics is becoming a commodity, but the permitting playbook and early option positions are not.
first_30_days: Sell five 'water-ready screening' reports at $15-25k to developers in the ERCOT queue and to towns, using public data only. Line up a drilling partner and identify two parcels near transmission with promising brackish aquifers to option.

title: Callback Verification Network for Invoice-Paying Agents
one_liner: A consortium ledger of verified vendor bank details plus automated out-of-band callbacks that gives accounts-payable agents a signed safe-to-pay attestation before they send money to changed payment instructions.
customer: Bookkeeping and AP-outsourcing firms (each managing 100-300 SMB clients) and AP-automation vendors first, then mid-market controllers ($50M-$1B revenue).
problem: Business email compromise costs roughly $2.8B a year in reported US losses. Humans used to catch odd bank-detail changes by accident, but an AP agent that reads emails and PDFs will follow an instruction injected into an invoice at machine speed (prompt injection maps to 6 of 10 OWASP agentic risks). The US has no Confirmation of Payee, unlike the UK (since 2020) and the EU (Verification of Payee mandated from October 2025).
solution: An API the AP agent calls whenever bank details are new or changed. We match against a shared ledger of callback-verified details contributed by all customers, run TIN and account-ownership checks, and if still unverified place an outbound voice-agent call to the number on file from the last verified contract or W-9, never the number on the invoice. We return a signed attestation that the payment policy requires, and anything unattested routes to a human. An optional guarantee covers attested payments.
why_now: Agentic AP is shipping in 2026, Nacha's 2026 fraud-monitoring rule phases push originators to prove controls, Google's threat group documents autonomous multi-agent credential harvesting in under 6 hours, and voice agents make a verification callback cost cents instead of a clerk's ten minutes.
revenue_model: $3-8 per new-or-changed-details verification, $0.15-0.40 per payment monitored, and a guarantee premium (about 1-3 bps of attested payment value) once loss data exists.
non_obvious_insight: Agents remove the accidental friction that used to stop fraud, so the defense that works is a channel the attacker and any injected prompt cannot touch. A shared ledger strengthens with every adopter, which builds Confirmation of Payee bottom-up in a country whose banks will not build it.
first_30_days: Sign 10 bookkeeping firms that together manage 1,000+ SMB vendors. Run callbacks semi-manually with a voice agent and humans on escalation, and sell a verified-vendor book at $99 per month per client. Wire a webhook into one AP tool (Bill.com or Ramp style) so the attestation gates payment approval.

title: GLP-1 Size-Curve Index for Apparel Planners
one_liner: A monthly 'size-shift index' that tells merchandise planners, airlines and furniture makers how GLP-1 adoption is moving their customers' bodies.
customer: Merchandise planners and size-curve analysts at apparel, footwear and outdoor brands and off-price retailers, plus airline, cruise, furniture and medical-equipment planners.
problem: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled to ~22%, and users lose double-digit percentages of body weight in a year. Retailers still plan size curves on last year's sell-through, which lags, causing markdowns on the wrong sizes. CFOs are already modeling downstream effects (Jefferies estimates ~$600M/yr airline fuel savings).
solution: Build an index by region, age and gender from licensed or partner data (pharmacy-fill proxies where affordable, retailer size and returns data, sizing surveys, public health data) and forecast size-curve migration by category. Deliver an API, a quarterly briefing, and a custom-model add-on.
why_now: Adoption accelerated after the 2026 pill launches. BCG and GoodRx data show measurable spend shifts (less pasta and bakery, more fragrance, skincare and supplements), so consumer-goods planners are hunting for leading indicators.
revenue_model: $40-120k/year per retailer or brand, plus $20-60k custom-modeling projects.
non_obvious_insight: Sell-through is a lagging indicator, and the drug adoption curve by ZIP is a leading one. It is a healthcare-adjacent data business with no clinical regulation if built on aggregated data, so a two-person team can sell it to non-healthcare budgets.
first_30_days: Build v0 from public data (NHANES, BRFSS, Google Trends) plus a 2,000-person sizing survey. Email 30 planners with a free size-shift report for one category and offer partner-data-in-exchange pricing. Sign one $15k pilot.

title: Childcare Credits Instead of Builder Rate Buydowns
one_liner: Homebuilders replace temporary mortgage rate buydowns with redeemable childcare credits, and the program builds the licensed care space inside the community.
customer: Small and mid-size spec and production builders with unsold inventory in family-heavy exurbs (Sunbelt and Midwest), and master-planned community developers. The end buyers are young families with kids under 5.
problem: 63% of builders use incentives and 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns with 30-year rates near 7%, yet completions fell 27.1% year over year. Buydowns are a one-time cost that fades in 2-3 years. For a household with toddlers, childcare ($13,128 per child, more than a mortgage for two kids in 45 states) is the actual affordability wall, and new suburbs are childcare deserts.
solution: The builder funds a Family Care Credit (for example $400 a month for 24 months) redeemable only at licensed providers in a vetted network. The startup pre-commits reserved occupancy with providers and helps a provider open in the community, using a builder-built care-ready clubhouse room, flex unit or model home at cost. The credit's cost accrues only when used, so expected builder spend can undercut a $12-20K buydown. Marketing kit: 'move-in ready, childcare included'.
why_now: Incentives are at a cyclical high, starts are steady but completions fell 27.1% and builders are financing shops. ROAD to Housing Act streamlining for small multifamily and factory-built homes aims at exactly these family starter products. Dependent-care FSA limits rose to $7,500, and childcare deserts are politically salient.
revenue_model: 10-15% program fee on credit dollars funded by the builder, per-family placement fee from providers, and later a margin on prepaid-slot financing.
non_obvious_insight: Builders see incentives as price cuts, but a family with a toddler values $400 a month of childcare more than a temporary rate cut. A builder is already a construction company, so converting a room to licensed space costs them little and is worth a rent-free facility to a provider. The guaranteed occupancy is what makes the provider's economics work in the first place.
first_30_days: Target five small builders with spec inventory in fast-growing exurbs. Check local childcare deserts with the CAP map, sign one builder for a 10-home pilot, and line up two licensed home providers. Launch a 'move-in ready with childcare' landing page and compare lead conversion to the builder's buydown ads. Have counsel confirm the credit's treatment against buyer-concession rules.

title: Orphaned Solar Lease Cleanup at Home Closings
one_liner: A closing-desk service that untangles orphaned solar leases, PPAs and UCC fixture filings on retirees' homes so sales and estates can close.
customer: Title and escrow companies, listing agents, elder-law attorneys and estate executors, who pay per closing (fee taken from sale proceeds). Secondary customers are the retired homeowners themselves and their adult children.
problem: Door-to-door and telemarketed solar leases and PPAs were sold at kitchen tables to retirees on 20-25 year terms. Each one usually leaves a UCC-1 fixture filing on the home. The lessor may since have gone bankrupt (Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 and its portfolio was sold and is now serviced by SunStrong; Mosaic and Sunlight failed earlier). Sales stall at the last minute because the buyer's lender wants the lease assumed or paid off and nobody can find the assignment chain, the current servicer or a payoff quote. Heirs inherit a lease on a dead parent's house, with monitoring dead and inverters failing. Homeowners rarely have copies of what they signed.
solution: A fixed-scope workflow. (1) Pull county and state fixture filings and reconstruct the chain of assignment. (2) Identify the current servicer and pull the contract. (3) Produce either a lender-ready transfer/assumption package with the buyer's credit-approval prep, or a payoff/buyout quote. (4) File the lien release. (5) Where the sales pitch looks deceptive or the lease unenforceable, hand off to a consumer attorney. A shared database of lessor entities, servicers and their turnaround times compounds as more closings run through it. The service is priced so title companies see it as saving their fee on a dying deal.
why_now: The Sunnova bankruptcy (filed June 2025, plan effective November 2025) created a live wave of stuck transfers, and multiple state AGs are investigating. The federal homeowner solar credit ended after 2025, pushing installers toward leases and PPAs, which let the company keep the tax credit. Leases signed in 2016-2020 are now reaching resale and probate age as the peak-65 cohort dies or downsizes.
revenue_model: Flat $750-$1,500 per closing, paid at settlement from proceeds. Title companies can take a $299/month priority-handling subscription. There is an optional buyout-negotiation success fee, and attorney referral fees where the state allows.
non_obvious_insight: The panels are not the blocker. The blocker is paperwork nobody can find: a recorded fixture filing and an assignment chain across three companies. Closers know it as the #1 surprise at the eleventh hour. Half the street signed in 2017 with a clipboard salesman and kept no copies. Whoever owns the lessor and servicer map, and the county filing pipeline, owns the unblock.
first_30_days: Pick one high-solar county in TX, FL, CA or AZ. Scrape recorded fixture filings by known lessors and cross-match them against new listings and probate filings. Call 15 title offices that have had a stuck solar closing and offer the first 3 at cost. Build template packages for the top 5 lessors and servicers. Partner with one elder-law attorney and one consumer-protection lawyer for hand-offs.

title: Transition Sponsor Radar for Strategic Breakthrough Awards
one_liner: A subscription and dossier service that maps each SBIR Phase II technology to the specific budget line, program office and person who could commit to a Program Objective Memorandum (POM), which the new $30M Strategic Breakthrough awards require.
customer: Phase II awardees in DoD-funded SBIR (thousands per year) that want Phase III or Strategic Breakthrough money, plus SBIR-focused VCs and advisors who decide which portfolio companies to back.
problem: Strategic Breakthrough awards run up to $30M over 48 months, but a company needs at least one prior Phase II, at least 100% matching funds from new private capital or non-SBIR government money, and, for DoD, a 'commitment for inclusion in a program objective memorandum' from the acquisition executive or higher. Agencies must contract within 90 days of a proposal. The technology is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is finding the one person with authority over a budget line, and knowing the POM calendar, since the POM is written 18 to 24 months ahead of the fiscal year. The public data (R-1/R-2 RDT&E exhibits, P-1 procurement lines, FPDS contracts, SBIR.gov awards) exists but is not indexed by technology.
solution: Build a searchable graph linking SBIR.gov Phase II abstracts to R-2 program elements, project numbers and named PEOs/PMs, and to FPDS Phase III contracts (where SBIR data-rights clauses appear). For each customer, produce a 'sponsor dossier': the top 5 program elements that could absorb the tech, the POM cycle dates, who to call, precedent Phase III transitions, and candidate match-fund sources. Add a monthly alert when a relevant program element grows or a new Phase III model contract appears.
why_now: The Strategic Breakthrough allocation (up to 0.50% of an agency's R&D budget where R&D exceeds $100M) takes effect in FY2026 and runs to September 30, 2031. Agencies must also create standardized Phase I/II/III model contracts and track direct-to-Phase-II, strategic breakthrough and Phase III awards in the database. Data on where transitions happen will become far richer as this reporting starts.
revenue_model: $12k to $20k per tech-specific sponsor dossier, paid partly from the $50k Phase II T&BA allowance. $1,500 per month subscription for alerts and updates. $5k per month for SBIR-focused VC funds screening deals. Success fee on Phase III wins (1% to 3%) as an optional add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not funding, it is a named budget-holder who will put a line in a POM, and that map is buildable from public documents no one has joined to SBIR data. S. 3971 Section 3 (new Section 9(ff)(3)) sets the $30M cap, 48-month term, one prior Phase II, 100% match, DoD POM-commitment requirement and 90-day contracting deadline. Section 6 requires 'simplified and standardized procedures and model contracts' for Phase III. Section 8 requires the database to track Phase III prime and subcontract awards. All at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm. The award-size thresholds the SBA gave for April 2026 ($323,090 Phase I, $2,153,927 Phase II without SBA approval, https://www.sbir.gov/about) show how small the normal awards are next to a $30M award, so the sponsor commitment becomes the step everyone is scrambling for.
first_30_days: Download the SBIR.gov awards dataset and the latest DoD RDT&E R-2 exhibits (comptroller.defense.gov). Use an LLM to embed and match 200 recent Phase II abstracts to program elements, then have a former acquisition officer sanity-check the top matches. Give 10 Phase II founders a free one-page 'sponsor map' for their own tech. Convert 3 of them to a $12k dossier. Pitch 2 SBIR-focused VC funds a paid pilot on their portfolio.

title: Landed-Cost Lock for Crowdfunding Creators
one_liner: A per-campaign engine that decides what each pledge tier really costs to land in each country (HTS class, duties, freight, platform and pledge-manager fees) and configures the tariff surcharge and shipping table before a creator commits.
customer: Kickstarter and Indiegogo creators in tabletop games and hardware who have raised or plan to raise $50K-$2M, especially China-manufactured products shipping to US backers. Payer is the creator, or the small publisher's ops lead.
problem: The de minimis exemption ended May 2, 2025, so every backer parcel from China is now dutiable. Kickstarter's Tariff Manager only collects a surcharge at pledge-manager checkout (US addresses only); it does not tell the creator what number to charge. Creators end up guessing, and publishers have shut or laid off staff over the resulting margin hits.
solution: A lightweight web tool plus human-reviewed audit. The creator uploads BOM, carton dimensions, weights and destination mix. The tool returns an HTS classification with duty scenarios (DDP vs DAP), a costed shipping table by country, a 20-30% contingency, net-of-fees margin by tier (platform fee plus payment fee of roughly 8-10%, plus the BackerKit or Gamefound fee), and the exact surcharge and copy for the backer update. It adds an address-validation and duty pre-flight on the pledge-manager export.
why_now: US tariff and de minimis rule changes in 2025 are still moving through 2026, and Kickstarter launched Tariff Manager as a collection-only feature. Freight remains volatile. Creators now need a decision layer, not a checkout field, and the incumbents in this space are fulfillment companies whose content is marketing rather than tools.
revenue_model: $750-$2,500 flat fee per campaign audit (pre-launch or mid-campaign), $99/mo post-campaign ship-readiness subscription (address validation, duty pre-flight, surcharge reconciliation), and 0.25% of surcharges collected via the tool as an optional success fee.
non_obvious_insight: The platform solved collection but not decision-making. Kickstarter's own tariff guidance says "someone has to pick up the tariff tab. It might be you, your manufacturer, or your backers" (https://updates.kickstarter.com/shipping-fulfillment-strategies-for-creators-facing-tariff-changes/). A 2026 analysis calls Tariff Manager "a collection tool, not a decision-making system" and warns that a surcharge added too early "can undercut the campaign's credibility" (https://blog.winsbs.com/2026/05/07/kickstarter-tariff-surcharges-board-games/). The cost of guessing wrong is large: 61% of funded projects ship late, French publisher FunForge absorbed roughly $250,000 of unexpected fulfillment costs on one campaign (https://updates.kickstarter.com/why-kickstarter-campaigns-fail-after-funding-and-how-to-avoid-it/), and Greater Than Games shut down blaming tariffs (https://www.tcf.team/blog/crowdfunding-in-2025). Creators pay for certainty.
first_30_days: Scrape live and recently funded tabletop and hardware campaigns whose updates mention "tariff" or "surcharge", and build a free public teardown of 20 of them (estimated landed cost vs price). Cold-email each creator their own teardown with an offer to run the real audit for $750. Partner with one customs broker for HTS review and one pledge-manager consultant for referrals. Close 5 paid audits and productise the recurring spreadsheet logic into a simple web form.

title: Bank-Accepted $1,500 Diligence for Main Street Deals
one_liner: A fixed-price, CPA-signed mini quality-of-earnings pack that brokers attach to sub-$1M business listings so SBA lenders and first-time buyers can close deals that currently die at diligence.
customer: Business brokers listing $150K-$1M cash-flow businesses (pay about $995 per listing to pre-certify), first-time individual buyers (pay $1,500 at letter of intent), and community-bank SBA lenders who accept the format.
problem: Boomer-owned Main Street businesses (HVAC, laundromats, landscaping, small clinics) sell on seller-supplied P&Ls and add-backs because a real quality-of-earnings review costs roughly $15K-50K (prior knowledge), which is more than many deals can bear. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M companies, so no formal capital or diligence product exists below $1M (brief inference). Deals die late or close on bad numbers.
solution: A five-day standardized pack. AI ties out bank feeds, POS data and sales-tax filings to IRS tax transcripts (hard to forge), samples add-backs, checks customer and revenue concentration, runs a reviews-and-traffic authenticity check (bought reviews and followers inflate perceived brand value), scans liens, licenses and litigation, and produces an owner-dependence score. A partner CPA reviews and signs. The signed pack attaches to the listing and is reusable across buyers.
why_now: SBA loosened acquisition financing on 2026-07-04 (7(a) and 504 loans can be combined for up to $10M of SBA-backed financing). AI-forged P&Ls and bank-statement PDFs are now trivial to produce (prior knowledge), so lenders and buyers need evidence that survives forgery. CPA supply is flat at about 678K, so cheap AI tie-out plus a reviewing CPA is the only way to serve small deals. Bench's Dec 2024 collapse showed sellers' books can be trapped inside a vendor.
revenue_model: $1,500 buyer-paid report or $995 broker pre-certification per listing, plus a $250 lender-portal fee. Roughly 3 CPA hours per pack plus software gives about 65% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: The deal-killer is not the price of diligence, it is that diligence gets redone for every buyer. Certifying the listing once turns a per-buyer cost into a per-listing asset that brokers will pay for because it buys deal certainty. Tax transcripts plus bank feeds are also the only evidence AI cannot cheaply fake.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 freelance ex-QoE CPAs and ask 5 regional business brokers for active listings. Run 10 free packs in exchange for case studies and lender feedback, then charge $995 per listing. Walk the format past 2 SBA Preferred Lenders at community banks so 'lender-accepted' is true by month 3.

title: Camera-Free Nap-Room Proof-of-Supervision
one_liner: Start with NFC crib tags that create tamper-evident safe-sleep check logs for childcare centers, then add 60GHz radar that verifies presence and breathing without any camera.
customer: Childcare centers' infant and toddler rooms, small chains, childcare liability insurers and brokers, and licensing agencies.
problem: Safe-sleep checks are handwritten logs that can be filled in after the fact. Sleep supervision failures drive licensing violations, insurance claims and tragedies. Cameras raise privacy objections. After abuse incidents at premium chains (Bright Horizons NYC, per the brief), parents and insurers want proof that supervision happened, not just cameras.
solution: Phase 1: teachers tap a badge on an NFC tag at each crib every interval, producing a timestamped, tamper-evident log and alerts for missed checks. Phase 2: a ceiling-mounted mmWave radar puck detects presence, motion and position class with no images, cross-checking the log. Positioned as compliance logging, not a medical device.
why_now: Low-cost 60GHz radar chips and infant-sensing research are now mature. Insurers are tightening abuse and molestation coverage (from memory). Public attention to childcare safety is high after the 2025-26 incidents.
revenue_model: $20-45 per crib per month plus a $150 radar device, with insurer premium-credit revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The value is proof of supervision, not detection. Detection claims invite FDA regulation and false-assurance liability, while insurers and inspectors will pay for un-fakeable evidence that checks happened.
first_30_days: Build the NFC tag and phone app. Pilot in 3 infant rooms. Talk to 2 childcare insurers or brokers about premium credits. Prototype breathing detection on an evaluation radar board with adult volunteers and a manikin, never infants.

title: Backyard Telescopes as Cubesat Finders
one_liner: Pay owners of consumer smart telescopes to image newly deployed smallsats, so operators learn which object is theirs and whether their panels deployed.
customer: University teams, startups and small operators flying on rideshare missions with 100+ payloads, plus satellite insurers and brokers who want an independent health signal.
problem: After rideshare deployments the public catalog lags days to weeks and objects are mis-associated. A silent satellite may be dead or merely misidentified, and operators without their own ground networks burn weeks of contact attempts. 2025 saw 321 orbital launches and 4,517 satellites deployed, so far more unfunded small operators face this.
solution: A client for popular smart telescopes (Seestar and Unistellar class) receives tasking for predicted twilight passes and uploads wide-field frames. The server solves streak astrometry and photometry, returning position updates to improve the operator's orbit, an ID confirmation, and tumble rate and brightness changes that hint at panel or antenna deployment. Owners are paid credits per validated pass, with leaderboards.
why_now: Rideshare cadence and cheap launch flood the catalog with small, poorly funded payloads. Thousands of app-controlled smart telescopes now sit in backyards, AI streak detection is cheap, and the brief flags rising conjunction-screening load for operators.
revenue_model: $1,500-4,000 per mission for a LEOP identification and deployment package, plus a $500 per month monitoring subscription. About a third of revenue goes to observer payouts, and insurers pay per-object fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a fast, independent 'is it alive and deployed?' second opinion, not images. Space-situational-awareness firms build expensive sensor networks, whereas hobbyists supply sensors that are paid for in status and gear credits, at a fraction of the cost.
first_30_days: Use open-source astrometry and streak tools. Recruit 150 smart-telescope owners in maker forums and Discords. Take the public payload list of the next rideshare mission, cold-email 3 small operators with a free pilot, and convert two to paid at $1,500 on the following mission.

title: Drought-to-Curtailment Forecasts for Hydro-Powered Compute
one_liner: A subscription index that forecasts 30-180 day power-curtailment risk for bitcoin miners and AI data centers on hydro-dependent grids, built from rainfall, inflow and reservoir signals.
customer: Bitcoin mining hosts and data-center operators in hydro-heavy grids (East Africa, southern Africa, Central Asia, Paraguay, Pacific Northwest), plus their lenders, equipment financiers and insurers. Operators and lenders pay.
problem: Step one: Ethiopia cut power to miners by 75% during an El Nino drought, when reservoir inflows fell about 20% in a month. Miners use over a third of a grid that is 90% hydro. Step two: every hydro grid with growing crypto and AI load faces the same triage. Step three: hosts and lenders are financing sites on 'firm cheap green power' contracts with no drought-risk model.
solution: Combine satellite rainfall, soil moisture, snowpack, ENSO outlooks and satellite-measured reservoir levels into a probability of curtailed hours per site. Map it to each grid's known dispatch rules. Backtest against Ethiopia 2026 and the 2024 Kariba (Zambia/Zimbabwe) load-shedding. Deliver a weekly dashboard and a lender-diligence report.
why_now: El Nino drought is live, WMO calls this one of the driest years for the world's rivers in 35 years, and compute loads are chasing cheap hydro. Grids have now made compute-versus-water triage an explicit decision.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per operator portfolio, $10-30k per lender or insurer diligence report, and later an index licensed for parametric cover.
non_obvious_insight: The risk being mispriced is hydrological, not political, and the party who needs the forecast is the compute host's lender, not the grid. A dry year is a correlated credit event across every hydro-powered site.
first_30_days: Build a public-data prototype for five reservoirs. Publish a free weekly brief aimed at miners and hosting firms. Backtest and publish the Ethiopia and Kariba case studies. Pitch three hosting firms and two mining lenders for paid pilots.

title: Infection-Safe Energy Retrofits for Animal Shelters
one_liner: A shared-savings energy contractor that designs heat-recovery ventilation, heat pumps and batteries around shelter-medicine infection-control rules, funded by pet-welfare philanthropy and paid partly by utility resilience programs.
customer: Animal shelters, humane societies, boarding and daycare facilities and 24-hour emergency vet hospitals. Funders include pet-welfare foundations and utilities. The buyer is the shelter director or board, and the payers are philanthropy plus shared savings.
problem: Shelters must move a lot of conditioned air (guidelines commonly call for roughly 10-20 air changes per hour) to control respiratory disease, run heavy laundry and hot-water loads 24/7, and cannot go dark in a heat wave or outage. Utility rates rose 7.3% in a year. Most are nonprofits in old buildings, and energy contractors either cut ventilation (raising disease risk) or refuse the job. Meanwhile pet philanthropy is arriving but is aimed at care, not capex (Duffield's $250M over 5 years starts with 250 x $10K grants).
solution: A standard package built around air-change and zoning constraints: energy-recovery ventilation, heat pump water heaters for laundry, right-sized battery and optional solar with a critical-load panel. It is financed by grants, utility rebates, elective-pay tax credits where still eligible (to be verified per project) and shared savings. Shelters also commit to serve as pet-inclusive cooling or warming refuge in emergencies, with a utility or city paying an availability fee.
why_now: Duffield's $250M commitment (September 17, 2026) and PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge put unprecedented money into shelters. Electricity prices, storage costs (about $70/kWh packs) and utility resilience programs make small batteries viable, and no vendor has encoded shelter-medicine ventilation rules.
revenue_model: Design and project-management fee of 8-12% on $60-250K retrofits, plus a 20-30% share of verified savings for 7-10 years on projects financed by grant or green-loan capital, plus utility or city availability payments for refuge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint in a shelter is infection control, not kWh. The first vendor that treats ventilation and cross-contamination as design rules owns a trusted niche, and philanthropy has cash but no capex vehicle for energy.
first_30_days: Offer 10 shelters free utility-bill audits and publish an anonymized shelter energy benchmark. Help 3 of them use first-round philanthropic grants to fund detailed audits. Close one small paid project (heat pump water heaters for laundry) to build a case study. Talk to two utilities about a refuge availability payment.

title: Live-In Guardians for Probate Houses
one_liner: Vetted live-in 'guardians' keep a house occupied while an estate is in probate, so the executor keeps insurance validity, avoids vacancy losses and pays less than for a vacant-home policy.
customer: Executors, estate and probate attorneys, professional fiduciaries and out-of-state heirs holding an inherited house. Attorneys are the channel, and executors and estates pay.
problem: Probate sales often take 6 to 12 months or longer. Most homeowners policies limit or exclude coverage after 30 to 60 days of vacancy, so a burst pipe, vandal or squatter can leave the estate uncovered, and specialty vacant-home policies cost far more. The executor is a non-expert with fiduciary liability, often living out of state, and has no one to check the house.
solution: Place screened guardians (night-shift nurses, travel clinicians, grad students, apprentice tradespeople) in probate houses under a state-specific license agreement rather than a lease. Guardians pay a low monthly fee, keep utilities on, handle mail and lawn, and file daily check-in logs. The estate gets an 'occupied' attestation accepted by a partner insurer or MGA, monthly photo reports, and a house that shows better at sale time. Upsell cleanout and staging at sale.
why_now: Boomer estates are moving through probate in growing numbers, and homeowners insurers are tightening on nonrenewals and vacancy. Housing costs are high enough that many good tenants will accept a small duty load for below-market housing. UK-style property guardianship exists for commercial buildings, but the US probate house niche is open.
revenue_model: Estate pays $250 to $500 per month service fee. Guardian pays a program fee. Carrier or MGA commission on the policy. Fees on cleanout, staging and sale-transition services.
non_obvious_insight: The customer isn't buying a house sitter; the estate is buying continued insurance validity and a checklist that satisfies a fiduciary. Occupied status changes the risk class of the asset for the whole probate period. Legal structure (license, not lease, chosen state by state) is the real product and the barrier to copycats.
first_30_days: Pitch 15 probate and estate-planning attorneys in one metro on a pilot for their next three vacant homes. Recruit guardians through hospital and travel-nurse groups. Have a landlord-tenant attorney draft the license and pick a landlord-friendly state to start (for example Texas or Tennessee). Line up a vacant-dwelling insurance broker who will recognize the guardian arrangement. First revenue within about six weeks.

title: Staffed Junk Playgrounds as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Adventure playgrounds with loose parts, dirt, tools and trained playworkers, installed on unused lots at family-heavy apartment communities and sold to landlords as a renewal lever.
customer: Owners and operators of garden-style, suburban and build-to-rent multifamily communities (200+ units, many households with children ages 5-12). Parents are the secondary payers via optional drop-in fees.
problem: Roughly 40 states now require schools to restrict phones, yet the 3-6pm window at home is where screen time actually happens. Australia's under-16 social media ban has reportedly changed daily use only slightly (about 58% still use daily vs about 60% before), a sign that removing a device without providing somewhere to go does little. Parents want unsupervised, physical, unstructured play but fear liability and have no safe place. Meanwhile landlords spend amenity budgets on gyms and coworking rooms nobody uses and lose family tenants to turnover that costs thousands of dollars per unit.
solution: A turnkey adventure playground service in the UK 'playwork' tradition: pallets, tires, rope, cardboard, sand, water, hammers and a supervised fire pit on an old parking lot or lawn, run 15-20 hours a week (after school and weekends) by trained playworkers who intervene as little as possible. The operator supplies the loose-parts kit, a written risk-benefit assessment, staff training, a background-check protocol and a specialty liability policy. The property signs a monthly contract, and families pay nothing or a small add-on. Tracked outcomes include tenant survey scores and renewal rates for families with school-age children.
why_now: Phone-free school laws spread across about 40 states by mid-2026 and the 'anxious generation' framing turned play-based childhood into a mainstream parenting goal. Free-range parenting statutes in a growing number of states reduce neglect-law fear. Build-to-rent operators are competing on amenities and retention. Nonprofit adventure playgrounds exist but cannot scale because of staffing and liability, which a landlord-funded model solves.
revenue_model: Service contract of about $3-5k per property per month (staff, materials, insurance, management), optional $15-20 per child drop-in for non-residents, and multi-property master agreements with regional operators. Ten properties gives roughly $400-600k in annual recurring revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer of 'screen-free childhood' is the landlord, not the parent. One prevented move-out saves thousands of dollars in turnover, so a single retained family pays for a month of the program, and kids' friendships create lock-in that no gym can. The barrier to adventure playgrounds was never demand, it was insurance and staffing, and packaging them as a managed property service turns a nonprofit hobby into infrastructure.
first_30_days: Find one friendly 300-unit community and offer an 8-week free trial in exchange for data. Spend about $2k on pallets, tires, rope and tools, hire two playwork or early-childhood students, and get a liability quote from a specialty broker. Survey tenants with kids before and after, and track leasing-team feedback. Photograph everything and pitch 20 regional property managers through local apartment associations and LinkedIn. Aim to convert the trial and one more property to paid contracts within 4-5 months.
